title: Shared workspace move
scenario: An office coordinator and team representatives plan a trial move, distinguish temporary arrangements from permanent policy, and clarify equipment dependencies.
transcript:
[00:00] Harper: We need to plan the trial move into the east workspace. The trial is for one week so we can learn whether the arrangement works. This meeting is not a decision to close the current room or make the new seating plan permanent. I want that clear before we discuss logistics.
[00:28] Quinn: The east room has eight desks and one small enclosed room. The desks are installed, but two monitors have not arrived. Network access worked on the laptop I tested yesterday. That is one test, so I have not marked the whole room ready for everyone yet.
[00:54] Avery: Our team has six people who might use the space, but they will not all be there every day. I would prefer to let people say which days they expect to attend rather than assign them all a desk immediately. Some work needs a quiet call space, and some does not.
[01:22] Morgan: The enclosed room can help with calls, but we need a booking method. If it is first come, first served with no indication of when someone will finish, people may have to interrupt to find out. A simple shared schedule would make the arrangement more predictable.
[01:48] Harper: Let us use a shared schedule for the enclosed room during the trial. Morgan, please prepare that by Thursday. We are not establishing a permanent room policy today. The trial can tell us whether the schedule is useful and whether the room is available when people need it.
[02:15] Quinn: For the missing monitors, the supplier's estimate is Friday, but the shipment has not been confirmed. We could borrow two from the current room, though that would make it harder for people who remain there. I would rather keep the old room usable during the trial.
[02:41] Avery: I agree. Moving equipment out of the old room would make the trial less optional in practice. Could we start with six equipped desks and let people know that limit? If more than six want to attend on a day, we should resolve it before they arrive.
[03:07] Harper: Yes. The trial starts with six equipped desks unless the extra monitors arrive and are tested beforehand. The current room keeps its equipment. Avery will collect intended attendance by Friday noon. If there is more demand than space, we will discuss it with the people involved rather than assume who should stay away.
[03:36] Morgan: What day are we actually starting? The calendar invitation says Monday, but the checklist has a network test scheduled Monday afternoon. If that test is required before the move, the dates conflict. I do not want people to pack up on Monday morning while the room is still being checked.
[04:03] Quinn: That is an old checklist date. I can do the broader network test Thursday afternoon with three different devices, including a video call. I will also check the dock connections. Monday is feasible if those tests pass, but I cannot call it confirmed before that happens.
[04:29] Harper: Then Monday is the proposed start, conditional on Thursday's checks. I will send a go-or-delay update Friday afternoon. Until that update, people should not move equipment or assume the trial has started. If a check fails, we will agree a new date rather than quietly shift the start by a day.
[04:57] Avery: For the attendance question, can we also ask about practical setup needs? I am thinking of monitor height, a place to take calls, or whether written directions to the room would help. We should not ask people to provide personal explanations just to make the trial usable.
[05:23] Morgan: Yes, but keep that information out of the public attendance grid. People can send practical requests to Harper directly. The shared grid only needs names and intended days. Otherwise an ordinary scheduling document could become a place where preferences are discussed by everyone unnecessarily.
[05:48] Harper: Agreed. Avery will ask for intended days and tell people they can contact me about practical arrangements. I will respond individually. We are not promising every arrangement is already available, and nobody needs to explain a diagnosis or personal circumstance to ask a practical question.
[06:13] Quinn: There is also a storage cabinet with no labels. I can label shelves for shared adapters and cables. I do not think we should move personal belongings into it during a one-week trial, because we have not decided who has access or how storage will work longer term.
[06:40] Harper: Use it for shared equipment only during the trial. Leave personal storage undecided. Please label the shelves before Friday's update so the arrival instructions can say where common equipment is kept. We will not treat an empty shelf as an invitation to leave private documents there.
[07:06] Morgan: I can write a one-page arrival guide with the route, desk count, enclosed-room schedule, and who to contact about a problem. Would a floor plan be useful? I can add one, but we need written directions too so the map is not the only way to find the room.
[07:33] Avery: Please include both if the plan is simple, with written directions as the primary explanation. The east and west entrances are easy to mix up. Say which entrance the route starts from, and avoid phrases like go over there that only make sense during a tour.
[07:59] Harper: Morgan, send the guide draft Thursday evening. Quinn can check the equipment details Friday morning, and I will include the final version in the Friday update if we proceed. Keep the proposed Monday date labelled as provisional until I confirm the checks have passed.
[08:24] Quinn: I can do that. My final tasks are the network and dock checks Thursday afternoon, shelf labels before Friday, and guide review Friday morning. If the monitors arrive, I will test them separately. Their delivery does not automatically increase usable desk capacity until they work with the docks.
[08:51] Avery: How will we evaluate the trial afterward? I do not want the only question to be whether people liked it. We should ask what work the space supported, where they had to move elsewhere, and what information or equipment was missing. That would lead to specific changes.
[09:17] Harper: Those are good questions. We will use them at the end of the trial, with written feedback available as well as discussion. I will draft the feedback note. We have not set the review meeting time, and a one-week trial does not commit us to extending it.
[09:43] Morgan: I have the room schedule for Thursday and the arrival guide Thursday evening. I will describe the trial arrangements as temporary. There is no decision about permanent seats, personal storage, or closing the old room, so those should not appear as instructions in the guide.
[10:08] Harper: Exactly. Six equipped desks for now, old room retained, scheduled use of the enclosed room, and a conditional Monday start. I send the decision Friday afternoon after the checks and attendance count. Permanent arrangements remain open. Thanks for catching the timing conflict; that finishes our planning call.
